claim: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is a vascular sarcoma that metastasizes early in its clinical course and lacks an effective medical therapy.
source: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is a vascular sarcoma that metastasizes early in its clinical course and lacks an effective medical therapy.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the clinical characteristics of EHE, representing established knowledge about this disease.

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 are chimeric transcription factors and initiating oncogenic drivers of EHE.
source: The TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 fusion proteins are chimeric transcription factors and initiating oncogenic drivers of EHE.
evidence: This statement from the abstract characterizes the fusion proteins as chimeric transcription factors and oncogenic drivers, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: YEATS2 and ZZZ3, components of the ATAC complex, are key interactors of both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 fusion proteins.
source: A combined proteomic/genetic screen in human cell lines identified YEATS2 and ZZZ3, components of the Ada2a-containing histone acetyltransferase (ATAC) complex, as key interactors of both fusion proteins despite the dissimilarity of the C terminal fusion partners CAMTA1 and TFE3.
evidence: This claim is supported by BioID mass spectrometry data (Figure 6) and RNAi screen results (Figure 7) presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fusion proteins drive a unique transcriptome by simultaneously hyperactivating a TEAD-based transcriptional program and modulating the chromatin environment via interaction with the ATAC complex.
source: Integrative next-generation sequencing approaches in human and murine cell lines showed that the fusion proteins drive a unique transcriptome by simultaneously hyperactivating a TEAD-based transcriptional program and modulating the chromatin environment via interaction with the ATAC complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq (Figure 3), ChIP-Seq (Figure 4), and ATAC-Seq (Figure 5) data showing transcriptional changes and chromatin modifications.

claim: The ATAC complex is a key oncogenic driver and unifying enzymatic therapeutic target for EHE.
source: Interaction of the ATAC complex with both fusion proteins indicates that it is a key oncogenic driver and unifying enzymatic therapeutic target for this sarcoma.
evidence: This claim is based on the functional data showing that knockdown of ATAC complex components reduces anchorage-independent growth (Figure 7) and alters the transcriptome (Figure 8).

claim: The WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion is present in 85-90% of all EHE tumors.
source: The WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion is encoded by a t(1;3)(p36;q25) chromosomal translocation (Errani et al., 2011, Tanas et al., 2011; Tanas et al., 2016) resulting in a TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion protein present in 85–90% of all EHE tumors (Errani et al., 2011; Tanas et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that characterized the frequency of this fusion in EHE.

claim: Approximately 10-15% of EHE contain a YAP1-TFE3 gene fusion.
source: The other ~10–15% of EHE contain a t(X;11) (p11;q22) chromosomal translocation encoding a YAP1-TFE3 gene fusion (Antonescu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study that identified this fusion in a subset of EHE cases.

claim: TAZ and YAP are transcriptional coactivators that are nuclear effectors of the Hippo pathway.
source: In mammalian cells, the nuclear effectors of the Hippo pathway are TAZ (gene is WWTR1) and YAP, two paralogous transcriptional coactivators (Dong et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2007; Camargo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies that characterized TAZ and YAP as Hippo pathway effectors.

claim: Hippo signaling limits TAZ and YAP activity by phosphorylating various serine residues, promoting their accumulation in the cytoplasm and ubiquitin-mediated degradation.
source: Hippo signaling limits TAZ and YAP activity by phosphorylating various serine residues, promoting their accumulation in the cytoplasm and ubiquitin-mediated degradation (Dong et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the mechanism of Hippo pathway regulation of TAZ and YAP.

claim: TAZ and YAP bind to TEAD transcription factors to drive their transcriptional program.
source: In the nucleus, TAZ and YAP bind to the TEA domain (TEAD) family of transcription factors to drive their transcriptional program (Zhao et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that demonstrated the interaction between TAZ/YAP and TEAD transcription factors.

claim: TAZ and YAP have emerged as central oncoproteins in many different cancers.
source: TAZ and YAP have emerged as central oncoproteins (Harvey et al., 2013) in many different cancers including breast (Chan et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2012), colorectal (Wang et al., 2013), liver (Zender et al., 2006), lung (Xie et al., 2012), pancreas (Zhang et al., 2014), thyroid (de Cristofaro et al., 2011), and sarcomas (Fullenkamp et al., 2016; Merritt et al., 2018; Isfort et al., 2019; Eisinger-Mathason et al., 2015; Crose et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating oncogenic roles of TAZ and YAP in various cancer types.

claim: Point mutations within the Hippo signaling pathway are relatively rare in most cancers.
source: Despite this observation, point mutations within the Hippo signaling pathway are relatively rare in most cancers (Harvey et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review that characterized the mutational landscape of the Hippo pathway in cancer.

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 transforms cells by driving a predominantly TAZ-related transcriptional program that is mediated by binding to TEAD4.
source: TAZ-CAMTA1 transforms cells by driving a predominantly TAZ-related transcriptional program that is mediated by binding to TEAD4 (Tanas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors that characterized the mechanism of TAZ-CAMTA1.

claim: The ATAC complex primarily acetylates lysine 9 of histone 3 (H3K9) and to a lesser degree lysine 14 (H3K14).
source: The ATAC complex is one of two metazoan complexes that incorporates the GCN5 or closely related PCAF histone acetyltransferase subunit, and primarily acetylates lysine 9 of histone 3 (H3K9) and to a lesser degree lysine 14 (H3K14) (Nagy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study that characterized the enzymatic activity of the ATAC complex.

claim: YEATS2 has been shown to be functionally important to the pathogenesis of non-small cell lung cancer.
source: YEATS2, one of the subunits of the ATAC complex, has been shown to be functionally important to the pathogenesis of non-small cell lung cancer (Mi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study that demonstrated the role of YEATS2 in lung cancer.

claim: Amplification of YEATS2 has been identified in ovarian cancer, head and neck cancer, esophageal cancer, uterine cancer, and liposarcoma.
source: Amplification of YEATS2 has been identified in ovarian cancer, head and neck cancer, esophageal cancer, and uterine cancer (Mi et al., 2017), as well as both well-differentiated and dedifferentiated liposarcoma (Beird et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that identified YEATS2 amplification in various cancer types.

claim: The WWTR1-CAMTA1 gene fusion fuses the end of exon 2 or exon 3 of WWTR1 to a breakpoint with exon 9 of CAMTA1.
source: The WWTR1 (TAZ)-CAMTA1 gene fusion fuses the end of exon 2 or exon 3 of WWTR1 to a breakpoint with exon 9 of CAMTA1(2, 3).
evidence: This claim describes the molecular structure of the fusion, supported by previous characterization studies.

claim: The N terminus of TAZ contains the TEAD binding domain and 14-3-3 protein binding site.
source: The N terminus of TAZ contains the TEAD binding domain and 14-3-3 protein binding site (Kanai et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study that characterized the functional domains of TAZ.

claim: YAP1-TFE3 fuses exon one from YAP1 in frame to exon 4 of TFE3.
source: Similarly, YAP1-TFE3 fuses exon one from YAP1 in frame to exon 4 of TFE3 resulting in the N terminus of YAP fused in frame to the C terminus of TFE3.
evidence: This claim describes the molecular structure of the YAP-TFE3 fusion, supported by previous characterization studies.

claim: The N terminus of YAP contains the TEAD-binding domain.
source: The N terminus of YAP contains the TEAD-binding domain (Gaffney et al., 2012; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the domain structure and citation to a study that characterized YAP domains.

claim: The C terminus of TFE3 contains the transactivating domain, basic helix loop helix domain, and leucine zipper.
source: The C terminus of TFE3 contains the transactivating domain, basic helix loop helix domain, and leucine zipper (Antonescu et al., 2013; Kauffman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the functional domains of TFE3.

claim: TFE3 is a member of the MiTF family of basic helix-loop-helix containing transcription factors.
source: TFE3 is a member of the MiTF family of basic helix-loop-helix containing transcription factors, consisting of four structurally similar genes (TFE3, TFE3B, TFEC, and MITF), that are involved in regulating tissue-specific functions of cell differentiation (Kauffman et al., 2014; Steingrimsson et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the MiTF family of transcription factors.

claim: TFE3 activates transcription by binding to the µE3 motif within the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer.
source: TFE3 is ubiquitously expressed and activates transcription by binding to the µE3 motif within the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer (Beckmann et al., 1990; Henthorn et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the DNA-binding specificity of TFE3.

claim: TFE3 promotes cell survival in starvation conditions by regulating lysosomal biogenesis and homeostasis.
source: TFE3 has recently been shown to promote cell survival in starvation conditions by regulating lysosomal biogenesis and homeostasis while also having a role in clearance of cellular debris (Martina et al., 2014; Slade and Pulinilkunnil, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the cellular functions of TFE3.

claim: TFE3 is involved in gene fusions in renal cell carcinoma and alveolar soft part sarcoma.
source: TFE3 is also involved in gene fusions in renal cell carcinoma and alveolar soft part sarcoma (Kauffman et al., 2014; Argani et al., 2003; Klatte et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that identified TFE3 fusions in other cancer types.

claim: YAP-TFE3 promotes anchorage independent growth while full length YAP, full-length TFE3, or the truncated portions of YAP or TFE3 present in the fusion protein do not.
source: YAP-TFE3 promoted anchorage independent growth while full length YAP, full-length TFE3, or the truncated portions of YAP or TFE3 present in the fusion protein did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data (Figure 1B) and poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 1C, D) showing that only the fusion protein promotes anchorage-independent growth.

claim: YAP-TFE3 is a neomorphic protein combining properties of both YAP and TFE3 to transform cells.
source: The above findings indicate that YAP-TFE3 is a neomorphic protein combining properties of both YAP and TFE3 to transform cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that neither full-length protein nor truncated portions alone can recapitulate the transforming activity of the fusion.

claim: YAP-TFE3 remained predominantly nuclear under confluent conditions while YAP was enriched in the cytoplasm and its abundance was reduced.
source: Under confluent conditions, YAP was enriched in the cytoplasm and its abundance was reduced, while YAP-TFE3 remained predominantly nuclear (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1E-F) showing differential localization of YAP and YAP-TFE3 under confluent conditions.

claim: YAP-TFE3 remained in the nucleus upon cell confluence while YAP was no longer localized in the nucleus and instead accumulated in the cytoplasm where it was subsequently degraded.
source: Nuclear and cytoplasmic fractionation confirmed that YAP was no longer localized in the nucleus and instead accumulated in the cytoplasm where it was subsequently degraded. In contrast, YAP-TFE3 remained in the nucleus upon cell confluence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) showing differential localization and stability of YAP versus YAP-TFE3.

claim: YAP-TFE3 remained constitutively nuclear upon cell detachment while YAP localization shifted from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: Similarly, YAP localization shifted from the nucleus to the cytoplasm upon cell detachment, while YAP-TFE3 remained constitutively nuclear (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation data during a time course of cell detachment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).

claim: YAP-TFE3 is no longer subject to Hippo pathway-mediated suppression because the key residues targeted by LATS1/2 (S127 and S381) are not present in YAP-TFE3.
source: Taken together, the above data suggest that YAP-TFE3 is no longer subject to Hippo pathway-mediated suppression, likely because the key residues targeted by LATS1/2 (S127 and S381) (Zhao et al., 2007) are not present in YAP-TFE3.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that YAP-TFE3 remains nuclear under conditions that normally trigger Hippo pathway activation, combined with knowledge that key LATS phosphorylation sites are absent.

claim: Mice with NIH 3T3-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 demonstrated a shorter overall survival compared to empty vector.
source: Mice with NIH 3T3-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 demonstrated a shorter overall survival compared to empty vector (p<0.0001 for both YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data (Figure 1G) showing reduced survival in mice with fusion protein-expressing tumors.

claim: Time to tumor initiation was similar for NIH 3T3 cells expressing either YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion protein.
source: Tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 formed palpable masses ~ 7 days post-injection (Figure 1H) indicating time to tumor initiation was similar for NIH 3T3 cells expressing either fusion protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data (Figure 1H) showing similar kinetics of tumor formation for both fusion proteins.

claim: NIH 3T3 cells containing empty vector formed tumors, but tumor initiation was delayed by approximately 10 days compared to fusion protein-expressing cells.
source: NIH 3T3 cells containing empty vector formed tumors, as has been described (Greig et al., 1985), but tumor initiation was delayed by approximately 10 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data (Figure 1H) and citation to a previous study showing that NIH 3T3 cells can form tumors.

claim: The slopes of the growth curves for YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 were similar to empty vector, confirmed by Ki-67 labeling.
source: The slopes of the growth curves for the two fusion proteins were similar to empty vector, and this was confirmed by Ki-67 labeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data (Figure 1H) and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).

claim: NIH 3T3 cell-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 exhibited a more rounded (epithelioid) cytomorphology and a greater degree of cellular pleomorphism compared to control tumors.
source: NIH 3T3 cell-derived tumors expressing YAP-TFE3 or TAZ-CAMTA1 exhibited a more rounded (epithelioid) cytomorphology and a greater degree of cellular pleomorphism as compared to control tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis (H&E staining) shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Microscopic metastases were present in the lungs of mice with YAP-TFE3-expressing tumors but not TAZ-CAMTA1-expressing tumors.
source: Necropsy and pathological evaluation of the lungs demonstrated the presence of microscopic metastases in the YAP-TFE3 (p=0.0299) but not the TAZ-CAMTA1 (not significant) cohorts (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of lung tissue and quantification of metastases (Figure 1I).

claim: Expression of YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 decreased latency to tumor formation compared to empty vector in SW872 cells in vivo.
source: In the mildly tumorigenic SW872 cell line (Stratford et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013a; Li et al., 2014), expression of YAP-TFE3 and TAZ-CAMTA1 decreased latency to tumor formation compared to empty vector in vivo (Figure 1J), similar to NIH 3T3 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data for SW872 xenografts (Figure 1J).

claim: The S51A mutant of TAZ-CAMTA1 significantly reduced colony formation in soft agar and growth on poly-HEMA while the TAZ-CAMTA1ΔWW mutant did not.
source: While the S51A mutant (disrupts TEAD binding) of TAZ-CAMTA1 significantly reduced colony formation in soft agar/growth on poly-HEMA (Tanas et al., 2016), the TAZ-CAMTA1ΔWW mutant did not (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar and poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G) comparing different TAZ-CAMTA1 mutants.

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 function is dependent on the TEAD binding domain but not the WW domain.
source: This confirms that TAZ-CAMTA1 function is dependent on the TEAD binding domain but not the WW domain.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the differential effects of mutations in the TEAD binding domain versus the WW domain on TAZ-CAMTA1 function.

claim: Knock-down of Tead1 reduced anchorage independent growth on poly-HEMA and in soft agar in NIH-3T3 cells expressing YAP-TFE3.
source: Knock-down of Tead1 reduced anchorage independent growth on poly-HEMA (Figure 2B) and in soft agar (Figure 2C) with two different short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs).
evidence: This claim is supported by poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 2B) and soft agar assay data (Figure 2C) after Tead1 knockdown.

claim: The YAP-TFE3 S94A mutation completely abrogated YAP-TFE3-driven anchorage-independent growth on poly-HEMA and in soft agar.
source: The S94A mutation completely abrogated YAP-TFE3-driven anchorage-independent growth on poly-HEMA (Figure 2E) and in soft agar (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by poly-HEMA assay data (Figure 2E) and soft agar assay data (Figure 2F) comparing YAP-TFE3 to the S94A mutant.

claim: The YAP-TFE3 S94A mutant showed a sevenfold decrease in expression of Ccn2(Ctgf) compared to the YAP-TFE3 control.
source: By quantitative RT-PCR, the YAP-TFE3 S94A mutant showed a sevenfold decrease in expression of Ccn2(Ctgf), a YAP target gene, compared to the YAP-TFE3 control (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data (Figure 2G) comparing gene expression between YAP-TFE3 and the S94A mutant.

claim: YAP-TFE3 S94A showed a sixfold decrease in CCN2 promoter binding compared to YAP-TFE3 control by ChIP-qPCR.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation-quantitative PCR for the CCN2 promoter (which contains the TEAD-binding sequence) showed a sixfold decrease in CCN2 promoter binding by YAP-TFE3 S94A as compared to YAP-TFE3 control (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 2H) showing reduced binding of the S94A mutant to the CCN2 promoter.

claim: YAP-TFE3 S94A showed decreased luciferase activity compared to the YAP-TFE3 control using the 8XGTIIC luciferase reporter.
source: Using the 8XGTIIC luciferase reporter containing eight TEAD consensus binding sequences (Dupont et al., 2011), YAP-TFE3 S94A showed decreased luciferase activity compared to the YAP-TFE3 control (Figure 2I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data (Figure 2I) comparing YAP-TFE3 to the S94A mutant.

claim: YAP-TFE3, like TAZ-CAMTA1, requires TEAD transcription factors to drive its oncogenic transcriptional program.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that YAP-TFE3, like TAZ-CAMTA1, requires TEAD transcription factors to drive its oncogenic transcriptional program (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence showing that disrupting TEAD binding abolishes YAP-TFE3 function.

claim: 70% of genes differentially expressed in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome were also present in the TAZ4SA transcriptome.
source: Differentially expressed genes (FDR < 0.05) showed considerable overlap between the TAZ4SA and TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptomes; 70% of genes differentially expressed in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome were also present in the TAZ4SA transcriptome with a –log10[hypergeometric density] (HGD) of 105.6 (p=1.92×10−106).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the TAZ-CAMTA1 and TAZ4SA transcriptomes.

claim: 9% of genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome overlapped with the CAMTA1 gene set.
source: By comparison, a much smaller percentage of overlap (9%) was identified between the TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 gene sets with an HGD of 34.1 (p=4.71×10−35).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 transcriptomes.

claim: 29% of differentially expressed genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptional program in NIH 3T3 cells were not induced by either TAZ4SA or CAMTA1.
source: A significant percentage (29%) of differentially expressed genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptional program were not induced by either TAZ4SA or CAMTA1 (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1) in NIH 3T3 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3A) showing unique genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome.

claim: 31% of the TAZ-CAMTA1 gene set in SW872 cells were unique and not found in the TAZ or CAMTA1 transcriptional programs.
source: Similarly, 31% of the TAZ-CAMTA1 gene set in SW872 cells were unique and not found in the TAZ or CAMTA1 transcriptional programs (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3B) showing unique genes in the TAZ-CAMTA1 transcriptome in SW872 cells.

claim: 78% of genes differentially expressed in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome in NIH 3T3 cells were present in the YAP5SA transcriptional program.
source: In NIH 3T3 cells, 78% of genes differentially expressed in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome were present in the YAP5SA transcriptional program.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the YAP-TFE3 and YAP5SA transcriptomes.

claim: 10% of differentially expressed genes in the YAP-TFE3 gene set in NIH 3T3 cells were also present in the TFE3 transcriptome.
source: Comparatively, only 10% of differentially expressed genes in the YAP-TFE3 gene set were also present in the TFE3 transcriptome.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis comparing the YAP-TFE3 and TFE3 transcriptomes.

claim: 20% of the differentially expressed genes in NIH 3T3 cells were unique to the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not found in the YAP5SA or TFE3 transcriptional programs.
source: In NIH 3T3 cells 20% of the differentially expressed genes were unique to the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not found in the YAP5SA or TFE3 transcriptional programs (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3C) showing unique genes in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome.

claim: 47% of the YAP-TFE3 transcriptional program in SW872 cells was found only in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not in YAP5SA or TFE3 controls.
source: Similarly, in SW872 cells 47% of the YAP-TFE3 transcriptional program was found only in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome and not in YAP5SA or TFE3 controls (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3D) showing unique genes in the YAP-TFE3 transcriptome in SW872 cells.

claim: The TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes in NIH 3T3 cells grouped more closely together than the transcriptomes of their cognate full length proteins.
source: A principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes in NIH 3T3 cells grouped more closely together than the transcriptomes of their cognate full length proteins (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3E) showing clustering of samples.

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promote upregulation of the well-defined TAZ/YAP transcriptional targets CCN2(CTGF)/Ccn2 and CCN1(CYR61)/Ccn1.
source: This was corroborated by qRT-PCR experiments, which showed that TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promote upregulation of the well-defined TAZ/YAP transcriptional targets CCN2(CTGF)/Ccn2 and CCN1(CYR61)/Ccn1, but also genes unique to the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes such as Fras1 (an extracellular matrix protein), Erbb3 (Erb-B2 Receptor Tyrosine Kinase 3) (Figure 3F), and FBLN5 (an extracellular matrix protein) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR validation data (Figure 3F and 3G) confirming RNA-Seq findings.

claim: The top cancer-related signatures activated by TAZ-CAMTA1 in SW872 cells are the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, Hippo signaling pathway, focal adhesion, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction.
source: iPathwayGuide analysis performed showed that the top cancer-related signatures activated by TAZ-CAMTA1 in SW872 cells (Figure 3H) are the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, Hippo signaling pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), focal adhesion, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix (ECM)-receptor interaction (mirroring qRT-PCR results in Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3H) showing enriched pathways.

claim: The top cancer-related signatures activated by YAP-TFE3 in SW872 cells included the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, MAPK signaling pathway, and JAK-STAT signaling pathway.
source: The top cancer-related signatures activated by YAP-TFE3 in SW872 cells (Figure 3I) also included the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, as well as the MAPK and JAK-STAT signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 3I) showing enriched pathways.

claim: CAMTA1 and TFE3 ChIP peaks were localized in closer proximity to the TSS (0-1 kb) compared to TAZ4SA, TAZ-CAMTA1, YAP5SA, and YAP-TFE3.
source: Annotation of ChIP peaks with respect to their nearest gene transcriptional start site (TSS) demonstrated that CAMTA1 and TFE3 ChIP peaks were localized in closer proximity to the TSS (0–1 kb). In contrast, TAZ4SA, TAZ-CAMTA1, YAP5SA, and YAP-TFE3 predominantly occupied distal intergenic sequences (3 kb or greater) consistent with active enhancer sequences (Figure 4A–E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis showing the distribution of binding sites relative to the TSS (Figure 4A-E).

claim: 69% of TAZ-CAMTA1 distal intergenic sequences overlap with H3K27ac ChIP peaks.
source: as confirmed by the presence of overlapping H3K27ac ChIP peaks (Zhang et al., 2013b; Creyghton et al., 2010; Calo and Wysocka, 2013) (69% overlap in TAZ-CAMTA1 distal intergenic sequences; 68% overlap in YAP-TFE3 distal intergenic sequences) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of overlapping ChIP-Seq peaks for TAZ-CAMTA1 and H3K27ac (Figure 4D).

claim: 68% of YAP-TFE3 distal intergenic sequences overlap with H3K27ac ChIP peaks.
source: as confirmed by the presence of overlapping H3K27ac ChIP peaks (Zhang et al., 2013b; Creyghton et al., 2010; Calo and Wysocka, 2013) (69% overlap in TAZ-CAMTA1 distal intergenic sequences; 68% overlap in YAP-TFE3 distal intergenic sequences) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of overlapping ChIP-Seq peaks for YAP-TFE3 and H3K27ac (Figure 4E).

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 maintain the genomic occupancy characteristics of increased preference for distal intergenic/enhancer sequences as demonstrated by TAZ and YAP, but also occupy sequences proximal to the TSS.
source: Thus TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 maintain the genomic occupancy characteristics of increased preference for distal intergenic/enhancer sequences as demonstrated by TAZ and YAP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C; Zanconato et al., 2015; Galli et al., 2015; Stein et al., 2015), but also occupy sequences proximal to the TSS.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis (Figure 4C-E) and citations to previous studies characterizing TAZ/YAP genomic occupancy.

claim: 56% of TAZ-CAMTA1 genes containing ChIP peaks were present in the TAZ-CAMTA1 data set, but not the TAZ4SA or CAMTA1 data sets.
source: Mirroring the RNA-Seq data, 56% of TAZ-CAMTA1 genes containing ChIP peaks were present in the TAZ-CAMTA1 data set, but not the TAZ4SA or CAMTA1 data sets (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4F) showing unique genes bound by TAZ-CAMTA1.

claim: 46% of YAP-TFE3 genes containing ChIP peaks were unique to the YAP-TFE3 data set and not present in the YAP5SA or TFE3 controls.
source: Similarly, 46% of YAP-TFE3 genes containing ChIP peaks were unique to the YAP-TFE3 data set and not present in the YAP5SA or TFE3 controls (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4G) showing unique genes bound by YAP-TFE3.

claim: The chromatin binding profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 more closely resembled TAZ4SA than CAMTA1.
source: Overall, the chromatin binding profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 more closely resembled TAZ4SA (HGD of 52.9) than CAMTA1 (HGD of 43.8).
evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ChIP-Seq data comparing the overlap between different datasets.

claim: YAP-TFE3 bound chromatin was more like that of YAP5SA than TFE3.
source: Likewise, YAP-TFE3 bound chromatin was more like that of YAP5SA (HGD of 166.8) than TFE3 (HGD of 11.8).
evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ChIP-Seq data comparing the overlap between different datasets.

claim: Approximately the same proportion of TAZ4SA and TAZ-CAMTA1 peaks contained the TEAD binding sequence (58% vs. 61%, respectively).
source: Unbiased motif enrichment analysis (Figure 4—source data 1) showed that approximately the same proportion of TAZ4SA and TAZ-CAMTA1 peaks contained the TEAD binding sequence (58% vs. 61%, respectively) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4F).

claim: There was a decrease in the frequency of FOS/JUN binding sites in TAZ-CAMTA1 (31%) as compared to TAZ4SA (50%).
source: Interestingly, there was a decrease in the frequency of FOS/JUN binding sites in TAZ-CAMTA1 (31%) as compared to TAZ4SA (50%), which appeared to be offset by an increase in Early growth response gene-2 (EGR2) binding motifs (23% vs. 13% for TAZ4SA).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: There was an increase in EGR2 binding motifs in TAZ-CAMTA1 (23%) compared to TAZ4SA (13%).
source: Interestingly, there was a decrease in the frequency of FOS/JUN binding sites in TAZ-CAMTA1 (31%) as compared to TAZ4SA (50%), which appeared to be offset by an increase in Early growth response gene-2 (EGR2) binding motifs (23% vs. 13% for TAZ4SA).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: The fraction of YAP-TFE3-bound peaks containing the TEAD-binding sequence (38%) was decreased compared to YAP5SA-bound peaks (51%).
source: Motif enrichment analysis showed a decrease in the fraction of YAP-TFE3-bound peaks containing the TEAD-binding sequence (38%) as compared to YAP5SA-bound peaks (51%) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4G).

claim: The MiTF binding motif was enriched in YAP-TFE3 (58%) compared to YAP5SA (16%).
source: Interestingly, the MiTF binding motif was enriched in YAP-TFE3 (58%) compared to YAP5SA (16%) (Figure 4G), suggesting that, like TAZ-CAMTA1, TFE3 confers DNA binding properties to the YAP-TFE3 protein in addition to events mediated by YAP's interaction with TEAD transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4G).

claim: YAP-TFE3 co-immunoprecipitates with TFE3.
source: Consistent with this, we found that YAP-TFE3 indeed co-immunoprecipitates with TFE3, and that disruption of the bHLH domain in the TFE3 portion of YAP-TFE3 that is responsible for dimerization altered anchorage-independent growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) showing interaction between YAP-TFE3 and TFE3.

claim: Disruption of the bHLH domain in the TFE3 portion of YAP-TFE3 altered anchorage-independent growth.
source: Consistent with this, we found that YAP-TFE3 indeed co-immunoprecipitates with TFE3, and that disruption of the bHLH domain in the TFE3 portion of YAP-TFE3 that is responsible for dimerization altered anchorage-independent growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) showing reduced colony formation with the bHLH domain mutant.

claim: 13% of differentially expressed genes for TAZ-CAMTA1 were directly bound by the transcription factor.
source: Thirteen percent of differentially expressed genes for TAZ-CAMTA1 were directly bound by the transcription factor (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).

claim: 15% of differentially expressed genes for YAP-TFE3 were directly bound by the fusion protein.
source: Similarly, 15% of differentially expressed genes for YAP-TFE3 were directly bound by the fusion protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ChIP-Seq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 preferentially opened chromatin in areas of the genome more distal to the TSS than TAZ4SA.
source: Heat map and histogram analysis of ATAC peaks showed that TAZ-CAMTA1 and CAMTA1 preferentially opened chromatin in areas of the genome more distal to the TSS than TAZ4SA (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-Seq data analysis (Figure 5A) showing the distribution of accessible chromatin relative to the TSS.

claim: YAP-TFE3 preferentially opened chromatin architecture more distal to the TSS than YAP5SA.
source: Similarly, although less pronounced, YAP-TFE3 preferentially opened chromatin architecture more distal to the TSS than YAP5SA (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-Seq data analysis (Figure 5B) showing the distribution of accessible chromatin relative to the TSS.

claim: The accessible chromatin profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 most closely resembled that of CAMTA1.
source: However, hypergeometric analysis showed that the accessible chromatin profile of TAZ-CAMTA1 most closely resembled that of CAMTA1 (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5C).

claim: The hypergeometric density between YAP-TFE3 and YAP5SA (106.0) was roughly equivalent to that between YAP-TFE3 and TFE3 (98.0).
source: while the -log10(hypergeometric density) HGD between YAP-TFE3 and YAP5SA (106.0) was roughly equivalent to that between YAP-TFE3 and TFE3 (98.0) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by hypergeometric analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5D).

claim: Both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promoted chromatin accessibility for unique genes not found in the control data sets.
source: This analysis (Figure 5C,D) also showed that both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 promoted chromatin accessibility for unique genes not found in the control data sets, making them available for either transcriptional activation or repression.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5C, D) showing unique accessible chromatin regions.

claim: More transposase accessible, non-baseline genes were present with expression of TAZ-CAMTA1 (3147 genes) and YAP-TFE3 (2499 genes) than TAZ4SA (656 genes) and YAP5SA (1629 genes), respectively.
source: More transposase accessible, non-baseline genes were present with expression of TAZ-CAMTA1 (3147 genes) and YAP-TFE3 (2499 genes) than TAZ4SA (656 genes) and YAP5SA (1629 genes), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ATAC-Seq data comparing the number of accessible chromatin regions across different conditions.

claim: TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 samples clustered together with CAMTA1 and TFE3 in PCA analysis of ATAC peak affinity patterns, while TAZ4SA or YAP5SA were distinct and separate.
source: 'Diffbind' differential binding affinity analysis of consensus-derived peak sets was carried out with respect to empty vector controls. Dimensionality reduction with PCA showed that TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 samples clustered together with CAMTA1 and TFE3, suggesting a greater degree of similarity in ATAC peak affinity patterns, while TAZ4SA or YAP5SA were distinct and separate (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5E) showing clustering of samples.

claim: The majority of genes bound by the fusion proteins, as well as those which were differentially expressed, were within euchromatin regions of the genome.
source: Integrating annotation results from all three NGS modalities (RNA-, ChIP-, and ATAC-seq) showed that the majority of genes bound by the fusion proteins, as well as those which were differentially expressed, were within euchromatin regions of the genome (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq, ChIP-Seq, and ATAC-Seq data (Figure 5F, G).

claim: The YAP-TFE3 proximity interactome was composed predominantly of histone modifying enzymes (35%), transcriptional regulators (26%), proteins involved in chromatin remodeling (18%), and transcription factor/co-activators (15%).
source: The YAP-TFE3 proximity interactome was composed predominantly of histone modifying enzymes (35%), transcriptional regulators (26%), proteins involved in chromatin remodeling (18%), and transcription factor/co-activators (15%) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by BioID mass spectrometry data analysis (Figure 6B) showing the functional classification of interacting proteins.

claim: The TAZ-CAMTA1 proximity interactome was composed predominantly of histone modifying enzymes (27%), transcriptional regulators (18%), transcription factor/co-activators (15%), and chromatin remodeling (13%).
source: Similarly, the TAZ-CAMTA1 proximity interactome was composed predominantly of histone modifying enzymes (27%), transcriptional regulators (18%), transcription factor/co-activators (15%), and chromatin remodeling (13%).
evidence: This claim is supported by BioID mass spectrometry data analysis showing the functional classification of interacting proteins.

claim: 27 prey proteins were shared between the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 interactomes after filtering.
source: We then retained only prey proteins that demonstrated an increased interaction with the fusion proteins relative to full length TAZ and YAP, leaving 47 proteins in the TAZ-CAMTA1 data set and 28 remaining proteins in the YAP-TFE3 data set. The two data sets were intersected to demonstrate 27 shared proteins (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis of BioID mass spectrometry data (Figure 6C-E) showing shared interacting proteins.

claim: The shared prey proteins between TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 were enriched for epigenetic/transcriptional regulators.
source: As shown in the table listing the function of the shared proteins (Figure 6D) and a chart giving an overview of their composition (Figure 6E), the shared prey proteins were enriched for epigenetic/transcriptional regulators.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional classification of shared interacting proteins (Figure 6D, E).

claim: YEATS2 and ZZZ3 are the two top ranking hits in the RNAi screen.
source: Significantly, YEATS2 and ZZZ3, the two top ranking hits in the RNAi screen, are both members of the Ada2a-containing histone acetyltransferase complex (ATAC).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNAi screen results (Figure 7C) showing that YEATS2 and ZZZ3 had the highest number of shRNAs causing a phenotype.

claim: YEATS2 is the scaffolding protein for other subunits of the ATAC complex and binds to H3K27ac via its YEATS domain.
source: YEATS2 is the scaffolding protein for other subunits of the ATAC complex and binds to H3K27ac via its YEATS domain (Mi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study that characterized the function of YEATS2 in the ATAC complex.

claim: The ZZ domain of ZZZ3 binds the histone H3 tail and in combination with YEATS2 anchors the ATAC complex to acetylated H3.
source: The ZZ domain of ZZZ3 binds the histone H3 tail and in combination with YEATS2 anchors the ATAC complex to acetylated H3 (Mi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study that characterized the function of ZZZ3 in the ATAC complex.

claim: GCN5 or the closely related PCAF subunit are responsible for acetylating H3K9, which subsequently opens the surrounding chromatin structure promoting transcription.
source: GCN5 or the closely related PCAF subunit (Nagy and Tora, 2007) are responsible for acetylating H3K9, which subsequently opens the surrounding chromatin structure promoting transcription (Mi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that characterized the enzymatic activity of GCN5/PCAF.

claim: KAT14, a third subunit of the ATAC complex, was identified by BioID mass spectrometry to interact with TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3.
source: In addition, KAT14, a third subunit of the ATAC complex, was identified by BioID mass spectrometry to interact with TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 (Figure 6C), further emphasizing the functional significance of this complex and an additional impetus to prioritize YEATS2 and ZZZ3 for further study.
evidence: This claim is supported by BioID mass spectrometry data (Figure 6C) showing KAT14 as an interacting protein.

claim: Knock-down of YEATS2 in SW872 TAZ-CAMTA1 cells resulted in loss of anchorage-independent growth by soft agar assay.
source: Knock-down of YEATS2 in SW872 TAZ-CAMTA1 cells was confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and resulted in loss of anchorage-independent growth by soft agar assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) after YEATS2 knockdown.

claim: Knock-down of ZZZ3 in SW872 TAZ-CAMTA1 cells resulted in loss of anchorage-independent phenotype by soft agar assay.
source: Similarly, knock-down of ZZZ3 in SW872 TAZ-CAMTA1 cells was confirmed by western blot (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C) and the loss of anchorage-independent phenotype was replicated by soft agar assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D) after ZZZ3 knockdown.

claim: KAT14 showed the strongest interaction with TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 by co-immunoprecipitation among the three ATAC complex subunits identified by BioID.
source: We then performed co-immunoprecipitation studies to validate the BioID experiments. Of the three subunits of the ATAC complex identified by BioID mass spectrometry, KAT14 showed the strongest interaction with TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E-G) validating the BioID results.

claim: Knock-down of YEATS2 and ZZZ3 altered both the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes, compared to shRNA control.
source: Principal component analysis showed that knock-down of YEATS2 and ZZZ3 altered both the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 transcriptomes, compared to shRNA control (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 8A) after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown.

claim: Knock-down of YEATS2 and ZZZ3 had a greater effect on the final transcriptional program of YAP-TFE3 than TAZ-CAMTA1.
source: Knock-down of YEATS2 and ZZZ3 had a greater effect on the final transcriptional program of YAP-TFE3 than TAZ-CAMTA1, likely reflecting the smaller number of epigenetic modifiers interacting with YAP-TFE3 as compared to TAZ-CAMTA1.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis (Figure 8A) and is an inference based on the observation that YAP-TFE3 interacts with fewer epigenetic modifiers.

claim: The most down-regulated genes after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown in TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 expressing cells showed an enrichment of extracellular matrix proteins (FBLN5, SPP1, GPC4, and LAMA1).
source: Aligning the most down-regulated genes for TAZ-CAMTA1 shYEATS2, TAZ-CAMTA1 shZZZ3, YAP-TFE3 shYEATS2, and YAP-TFE3 shZZZ3 revealed an enrichment of extracellular matrix proteins (FBLN5, SPP1, GPC4, and LAMA1) (Figure 8B and Figure 8—source data 1) and validated by qRT-PCR (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis (Figure 8B) and qRT-PCR validation (Figure 8C) after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown.

claim: MAPK signaling, a pathway significantly upregulated in SW872 YAP-TFE3 cells, was significantly down-regulated with YEATS2 knock-down.
source: iPathwayGuide analysis showed that MAPK signaling, a pathway significantly upregulated in SW872 YAP-TFE3 cells (Figure 3I) was significantly down-regulated with YEATS2 knock-down (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 8D) after YEATS2 knockdown.

claim: PI3K-Akt signaling, activated in SW872 cells expressing TAZ-CAMTA1 or YAP-TFE3, was decreased in SW872 cells expressing YAP-TFE3 and either YEATS2 or ZZZ3 shRNA.
source: Further, PI3K-Akt signaling, activated in SW872 cells expressing TAZ-CAMTA1 or YAP-TFE3 (Figure 3H,I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), was also decreased in SW872 cells expressing YAP-TFE3 and either YEATS2 or ZZZ3 shRNA (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by iPathwayGuide analysis of RNA-Seq data (Figure 8D) after YEATS2 or ZZZ3 knockdown.

claim: 71% of differentially expressed genes with YEATS2 knock-down were within euchromatin unique to YAP-TFE3 expressing cells.
source: We found that 71% of differentially expressed genes (DEG) with YEATS2 knock-down and 74% of DEG with ZZZ3 knock-down were within euchromatin unique to YAP-TFE3 expressing cells (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ATAC-Seq data (Figure 8E) after YEATS2 knockdown.

claim: 74% of differentially expressed genes with ZZZ3 knock-down were within euchromatin unique to YAP-TFE3 expressing cells.
source: We found that 71% of differentially expressed genes (DEG) with YEATS2 knock-down and 74% of DEG with ZZZ3 knock-down were within euchromatin unique to YAP-TFE3 expressing cells (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated analysis of RNA-Seq and ATAC-Seq data (Figure 8F) after ZZZ3 knockdown.

claim: Vitronectin was expressed in all EHE samples, but was essentially absent in epithelioid angiosarcoma and epithelioid hemangioma.
source: In contrast, VTN was expressed in all EHE samples, but was essentially absent in epithelioid angiosarcoma and epithelioid hemangioma (Figure 8H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 8H) showing vitronectin expression in clinical samples.

claim: Increased expression of YEATS2 predicted a poorer prognosis across different histological types of sarcoma.
source: Via Kaplan-Meier analysis, we showed that increased expression of YEATS2 (Figure 8I) or ZZZ3 (Figure 8J) predicted a poorer prognosis across different histological types of sarcoma, suggesting the ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas in addition to EHE.
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (Figure 8I) using TCGA sarcoma data.

claim: Increased expression of ZZZ3 predicted a poorer prognosis across different histological types of sarcoma.
source: Via Kaplan-Meier analysis, we showed that increased expression of YEATS2 (Figure 8I) or ZZZ3 (Figure 8J) predicted a poorer prognosis across different histological types of sarcoma, suggesting the ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas in addition to EHE.
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (Figure 8J) using TCGA sarcoma data.

claim: The ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas in addition to EHE.
source: Via Kaplan-Meier analysis, we showed that increased expression of YEATS2 (Figure 8I) or ZZZ3 (Figure 8J) predicted a poorer prognosis across different histological types of sarcoma, suggesting the ATAC complex may be a key oncogenic driver in multiple sarcomas in addition to EHE.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that YEATS2 and ZZZ3 expression predicts poor prognosis across multiple sarcoma types.

claim: The ATAC complex is a key epigenetic mediator of the oncogenic properties of both the TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 fusion proteins.
source: Here, we provide new insights into the endothelial cancer EHE by studying the disease defining fusion proteins TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3. We find that each fusion protein drives a related but distinct transcriptional program, which is underpinned by the fact that they both engage the genome at least in part via the TEAD transcription factors, as do wild-type YAP and TAZ. Mechanistically, using a paired proteomic and genomic screen, we identify the ATAC complex as a key epigenetic mediator enabling both TAZ-CAMTA1 and YAP-TFE3 to modulate the chromatin environment and transcription, thus transforming cells.
evidence: This claim is a summary statement supported by the combined results of BioID, RNAi screen, and functional assays presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ATAC complex represents a potential therapeutic target for EHE, regardless of which fusion protein it harbors.
source: Importantly, our study also indicates that the ATAC complex represents a potential therapeutic target for EHE, a sarcoma currently lacking an effective medical therapy, regardless of which fusion protein it harbors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that the ATAC complex is required for the oncogenic function of both fusion proteins.
